707-320: 707-320 has a longer fuselage than the 707-120 and 720, giving it a more stretched appearance along its entire length.
707-320 features four engines mounted in individual podded nacelles suspended beneath a swept low wing.
707-320 has a classic early-jet narrow-body fuselage profile that is long and slender, not wide or humped like later wide-body jets.
707-320 displays a conventional tail configuration with a single vertical fin and low-mounted horizontal stabilizer, unlike the Il-76’s T-tail.
707-320 has a pointed, streamlined nose characteristic of 1950s jet design, distinct from the blunter, more rounded noses of later Boeing jets.
707-320 uses turbofan engines housed in larger-diameter nacelles compared to the smaller turbojet nacelles on earlier 707-120 variants.
707-320 has a more curved fin and rudder profile than the DC-8’s straighter, more angular vertical stabilizer.
707-320’s main landing gear retracts into prominent fairings along the lower fuselage, not into the wing roots like many contemporaries.
707-320 has a low-wing configuration, contrasting sharply with the high-wing layout of the Il-76.
707-320’s cockpit windshield area is relatively small and compact compared to the larger, multi-pane windshields of modern airliners.
707-320 lacks an upper-deck hump or twin-aisle fuselage width, distinguishing it visually from later Boeing wide-bodies like the 747.
707-320 has a more substantial and slightly taller vertical fin than the shorter-fuselage 720 variant.
707-320’s wing sweep angle is moderate and consistent with early jet design, less pronounced than the highly swept wings of military jets like the Tu-16.
707-320’s engine nacelles are noticeably larger in diameter than those on the DC-8, especially the inboard pair.
707-320 has no cargo ramp or rear loading door, differentiating it from the Il-76’s large rear clamshell doors.
707-320’s fuselage cross-section is circular and narrow, unlike the broader, oval-shaped fuselage of the DC-8.
707-320’s horizontal stabilizer is mounted low on the aft fuselage, not at the top of the vertical fin like the Il-76’s T-tail.
707-320 has passenger boarding doors aligned along the forward and mid-fuselage, without the oversized cargo doors seen on military transports.
707-320’s wing has a clean, unswept trailing edge near the fuselage, unlike the more complex flap and slat arrangements on newer jets.
707-320’s fuselage landing-gear fairings are more elongated and sculpted than the simpler, bulkier fairings on the DC-8.
727-200: 727-200 has a longer fuselage than the 727-100, giving it a more stretched appearance compared to other early Boeing 727 variants.

727-200 has low-mounted swept wings attached to a narrow-body fuselage, unlike the higher-wing placement of the Tu-154.
727-200 has main landing gear housed in prominent fuselage-side fairings or sponsons near the wing root, a feature absent on the twin-engined 737-200.
727-200 has a relatively pointed nose and clean cylindrical fuselage profile, less bulbous than the Tu-154’s rounded nose and wider forward fuselage.
727-200 has a greater distance between the front and rear passenger doors than the DC-9-30, reflecting its longer cabin length.
727-200 has more cabin windows than the 727-100, providing a visual cue for its stretched fuselage variant status.
727-200 has a narrower fuselage diameter than the Tu-154, contributing to a slimmer overall silhouette.
727-200 has no winglets or blended winglets, unlike later 737 variants such as the 737-800.
727-200 has a single central tail engine intake feeding the center engine, whereas the MD-80 has only two side-mounted engines with no tail intake.
727-200 has a shorter overall length than the Tu-154, making it appear more compact despite sharing a trijet layout.
727-200 has a classic narrow-body airliner proportion with medium-length fuselage and balanced jet-era dimensions, unlike the stubbier DC-9-30.
727-200 has no dorsal fin extension above the vertical stabilizer, unlike the prominent dorsal fin found on the Tu-154.
727-200 has engine nacelles mounted directly on the aft fuselage without pylons, contrasting with the underwing pylon-mounted engines of the 737-200.
727-200 has a vertical tail that is taller and more slender than the broader, shorter tail of the DC-9-30.

727-200 has no auxiliary power unit (APU) exhaust visible on the upper rear fuselage, unlike the prominent APU exhaust on the Tu-154’s tailcone.
727-200 has a clean, uninterrupted fuselage underside with no ventral fins or strakes, unlike the Tu-154’s ventral fin beneath the tail.
727-200 has a narrower chord and less pronounced sweep on its horizontal stabilizer compared to the broader, more highly swept stabilizer of the MD-80.
737-200: 737-200 has a shorter fuselage than the 737-300 and 737-400 but longer than the 737-500.
737-200 features twin underwing turbofan engines mounted close to the wing and fuselage, giving it a low-slung stance.
737-200 has a low-mounted swept wing, characteristic of the entire Boeing 737 family.
737-200 uses older small-diameter, nearly circular turbofan nacelles unlike the flatter-bottomed nacelles of the 737-300 and later variants.
737-200 has fewer overwing emergency exits than the 737-300 and 737-400 due to its shorter fuselage.
737-200 has a conventional tail with a single vertical fin and low horizontal stabilizers.
737-200 has a rounded nose profile with the classic Boeing narrow-body cockpit window shape.
737-200 has main landing gear housed in visible fuselage-side fairings rather than large wing-body pods.
737-200 is a narrow-body airliner with one passenger deck and short-to-medium fuselage length.
737-200 has engines mounted under the wings, distinguishing it from the rear-fuselage-mounted engines of the Boeing 717.
737-200 has simpler, more compact engine-to-wing proportions compared to the stretched 737 Classics and NG variants.
737-200 has a shorter forward fuselage section ahead of the wing than the 737-400.
737-200 has a less tapered rear fuselage than the 737-500, reflecting its earlier design lineage.
737-200 has no winglets, unlike many later 737 variants including the 737-800.
737-200 has a relatively blunt, unextended tailcone compared to the elongated tailcone of the 737-400.
737-200 has a smaller vertical fin height relative to fuselage length than the 737-800.
737-200 has cockpit windows with a more upright, less raked forward slope than those on the Boeing 717.
737-200 has a narrower chord wing root section than the 737-400, contributing to its more compact appearance.
737-200 has only two main landing gear doors per side, whereas the 737-400 has three due to its longer gear stroke and extended fuselage.
737-200 has a shorter distance between the nose gear and main gear than the 737-400, reflecting its overall shorter airframe.
737-300: 737-300 has a fuselage length that is longer than the 737-200 but shorter than the 737-400.
737-300 features twin underwing turbofan engines mounted on a low-slung narrow-body fuselage.
737-300 uses CFM56 engines with characteristically flattened lower engine inlets, unlike the rounder inlets of the 737-200.
737-300 has a conventional tail configuration with a single vertical fin and low-mounted horizontal stabilizers.
737-300 exhibits the classic 737 nose profile with a rounded, compact flightdeck area and no eyebrow cockpit windows.
737-300 has a swept low wing with one engine mounted beneath each wing.
737-300 has a shorter fuselage than the 737-600, resulting in fewer passenger window bays.
737-300 has main landing gear that is relatively short, giving it a low stance on the ground.
737-300 has a cylindrical fuselage cross-section typical of single-aisle jetliners.
737-300 lacks the extended forward fuselage and stretched proportions seen on the 737-400.
737-300 has a medium-length fuselage that is distinctly shorter than the 737-400 but longer than the 737-500.
737-300 features the Classic-series larger CFM56 nacelles, distinguishing it from the smaller nacelles of the 737-200.
737-300 has a low-mounted horizontal stabilizer positioned at the base of the vertical fin.
737-300 has a compact cockpit section with no extended nose or raised flightdeck like later Next Generation variants.
737-300 has a wing root position aligned with the mid-fuselage, consistent across the Classic series.
737-300 has a single-aisle fuselage diameter that is narrower than wide-body aircraft but identical to other 737 Classics.
737-300 has a vertical fin with a straight leading edge and no raked tip, unlike some newer Boeing variants.
737-300 has a fuselage that tapers gradually toward the tail without the pronounced rear stretch of the 737-400.
737-300 has a nose landing gear positioned just aft of the cockpit, with a two-wheel configuration typical of Classic 737s.
737-300 has a wing sweep angle of approximately 25 degrees, matching other Classic 737 variants but differing from the 737 MAX.
737-400: 737-400 has a longer fuselage than the 737-300 with more cabin windows both ahead of and behind the wing.
737-400 features CFM56 engines with flattened lower nacelles, unlike the rounder JT8D nacelles on the 737-200.
737-400 has one overwing exit per side, matching the mid-length Classic 737 fuselage rather than the shortest 737-500.
737-400 displays the classic 737 cockpit window shape and nose contour, distinct from the more modern-looking 737-600.
737-400 has a swept low wing with engines mounted close beneath the wing, consistent with the Boeing 737 family.
737-400 has twin underwing turbofan engines on a low-slung narrow-body fuselage, distinguishing it from wide-body families like the 777 or A330.
737-400 has a conventional tail with a single vertical stabilizer and low-mounted horizontal stabilizers, unlike T-tail designs such as the MD-80.
737-400 has main landing gear housed in pods or fairings at the lower fuselage, not fully retracting flush into the wing roots.
737-400 has a relatively short nose gear giving the aircraft a low stance on the ground, characteristic of the Classic 737 series.
737-400 has a narrow-body fuselage with a six-abreast cabin cross-section, unlike the wider fuselage of the Airbus A320 family.
737-400 has a shorter fuselage than the 737-800 and lacks the extended rear fuselage and additional overwing exits found on that variant.
737-400 has no winglets, distinguishing it from later 737 Next Generation and MAX variants.
737-400 has a single passenger deck, unlike double-deck aircraft such as the A380 or 747.
737-400 has a short-to-medium fuselage length, placing it between the 737-300 and 737-500 in overall proportion but visibly longer than both.
737-400 has engine nacelles that sit closer to the wing underside without the pronounced forward extension seen on the 737-600.
737-400 has a wing root fairing shape typical of the Classic 737 series, smoother and less angular than the NG series.
737-400 has forward and aft boarding doors aligned with the wing’s leading and trailing edges, differing from the repositioned doors on the 737-600.
737-400 has a low-mounted horizontal stabilizer attached directly to the fuselage, not to the vertical fin like some regional jets.
737-400 has a fuselage cross-section diameter consistent with other Classic 737s, smaller than the stretched cross-section of the 737-900ER.
737-400 has no dorsal fin extension behind the vertical stabilizer, unlike the 737-800 and later variants.
737-500: 737-500 has a shorter fuselage than the 737-400 and visibly shorter than the 737-300.
737-500 features CFM56 engines with flattened lower nacelles, unlike the rounder engines of the 737-200.
737-500 has the classic 737 nose profile with flight deck windows arranged in a distinctive stepped configuration, differing from the smoother, more modern nose of the 737-600.
737-500 displays fewer cabin windows than the 737-300 and significantly fewer than the 737-400.
737-500 has overwing emergency exits positioned closer together due to its shorter fuselage length compared to the 737-400.
737-500 has twin underwing-mounted engines, consistent with all Boeing 737 family variants.
737-500 has a low-slung narrow-body fuselage with conventional tail assembly featuring a single vertical fin and low-mounted horizontal stabilizers.
737-500 has short-to-medium span swept wings with one engine mounted beneath each wing.
737-500 has main landing gear housed entirely within the fuselage belly, without large wing-body fairing pods.
737-500 has low ground clearance, making its engines appear closer to the ground than those of larger 737 variants.
737-500 has a circular cross-section fuselage typical of classic narrow-body jet airliners.
737-500 has a standard jet airliner nose profile with no winglets or blended winglets, distinguishing it from later 737 Next Generation variants.
737-500 has a shorter forward fuselage section ahead of the first door compared to the 737-300.
737-500 has a cockpit window layout with three forward-facing panes on the upper flight deck, matching the classic 737 design and differing from the 737-600’s updated glazing.
737-500 has engine nacelles that sit higher relative to the ground than those of the 737-200 due to its taller landing gear and redesigned pylon.
737-500 has a single-deck fuselage without a raised roofline or stretched upper lobe, unlike wide-body aircraft such as the Boeing 767.
737-500 has wing root fairings that are smaller and less bulbous than those found on the 737-600.
737-500 has a tailcone shape that tapers more gradually than the sharper taper seen on the 737-600.
737-500 has forward boarding doors spaced closer to the nose than on the 737-400, reflecting its reduced overall length.
737-500 has winglets absent entirely, distinguishing it visually from 737 Next Generation and MAX variants.
737-600: 737-600 has the shortest fuselage among all 737 Next Generation variants.
737-600 features underwing twin turbofan engines mounted close to the fuselage.
737-600 has a more swept wing than the 737-500 but less swept than the 737-900.
737-600 displays a taller vertical tail compared to the 737-500 and other Classic-series 737s.
737-600 has a low-slung narrow-body fuselage with engines appearing relatively close to the ground.
737-600 possesses a conventional tail configuration with a single vertical fin and low-mounted horizontal stabilizers.
737-600 has a stubby overall appearance due to its compact fuselage paired with large NG wing and tail surfaces.
737-600 is longer than the 737-500 but shorter than the 737-700, making it the second-shortest in the entire 737 family.
737-600 lacks rear fuselage-mounted engines, distinguishing it clearly from the Boeing 717.
737-600 has a swept low wing with one engine suspended beneath each wing.
737-600 features a single-aisle cabin cross-section visible in side profile as a narrow fuselage diameter.
737-600 has a relatively short forward fuselage ending in a rounded, non-stretched nose section.
737-600 shows two main landing gear struts positioned beneath the wings, typical of narrow-body jetliners.
737-600 has no overwing emergency exits, unlike the longer 737-700 and 737-800.
737-600 has a cockpit window layout consistent with other 737 Next Generation models, featuring a distinct curved windshield base.
737-600 has only one pair of passenger boarding doors on each side, located just forward and just aft of the wing.
737-600 exhibits the characteristic 737 NG winglet design, which differs from the blended winglets on later variants.
737-600 has a higher ground clearance for the engines than the original 737 Classics due to larger-diameter NG engines.
737-600 has a fuselage length that creates a noticeably shorter distance between the nose and the leading edge of the wing than the 737-700.
737-600 has a vertical tail fin that is taller and more slender than the 737-500’s, reflecting Next Generation family styling.
737-700: 737-700 has a fuselage length that is visibly longer than the 737-600 but shorter than the 737-800.
737-700 features a taller vertical tail than the 737-300 and 737-500.
737-700 has more highly swept wings compared to the earlier 737-300 and 737-500.
737-700 mounts two underwing turbofan engines positioned closer to the wing leading edge than on the 737-300.
737-700 has rounded, larger engine nacelles unlike the flatter-bottom nacelles of the 737-300.
737-700 has a single vertical tail with a more upright fin shape than the slightly raked fin of the 737-600.
737-700 has a low-mounted horizontal stabilizer set further aft on the fuselage than on the 737-500.
737-700 has a narrow-body fuselage with six-abreast cabin cross-section typical of Boeing 737 Next Generation models.
737-700 has main landing gear housed entirely in fuselage fairings without prominent wing-root gear pods seen on older 737 variants.
737-700 has a cockpit glazing profile with a more pronounced curvature than the flatter windshield of the 737-300.
737-700 has fewer passenger windows ahead of the wing than the 737-800.
737-700 has fewer passenger windows behind the wing than the 737-800.
737-700 has door spacing that appears more compact than the 737-800 due to shorter overall fuselage length.
737-700 has a nose section that tapers more gradually than the sharper nose of the 737-600.
737-700 has winglets that are taller and more slender than those retrofitted to many 737-500s.
737-700 has a wing root chord that is wider than the 737-600’s, contributing to its intermediate proportions.
737-700 has a forward fuselage stretch clearly visible ahead of the wing compared to the 737-600.
737-700 has an aft fuselage stretch clearly visible behind the wing compared to the 737-600.
737-700 has a lower-slung fuselage profile relative to the ground than wide-body Boeing airliners like the 777 or 787.
737-700 has a swept low wing with a distinct kink at the outboard trailing edge not present on the 737-300.
737-800: 737-800 has a fuselage length that is longer than the 737-700 but shorter than the 737-900.
737-800 features twin underwing turbofan engines mounted close to the fuselage.
737-800 has a low-slung narrow-body fuselage with a single vertical tail.
737-800 displays a conventional tailplane mounted low on the rear fuselage, not a T-tail.
737-800 has swept wings with one engine mounted beneath each wing.
737-800 has short main landing gear giving it a relatively low stance on the ground.
737-800 typically shows blended or split winglets, distinguishing it from earlier Classic 737 variants.
737-800 shares the same nose and tail shape as the 737-700 but has a longer cabin.
737-800 has full-size forward and overwing exit doors consistent with its mid-length Next Generation fuselage.
737-800 has longer, more balanced proportions than the stubby 737-600.
737-800 lacks the especially stretched look of the 737-900 while retaining NG family proportions.
737-800 has no winglets on early builds but most examples feature either blended or split winglets.
737-800 has a narrower fuselage cross-section compared to wide-body aircraft like the A330 or 777.
737-800 has a single-aisle cabin configuration visible through window spacing and door placement.
737-800 has two main landing gear struts, each with two wheels, positioned under the wings.
737-800 has a cockpit windshield with a distinctive curved, multi-pane layout shared across the NG family.
737-800 has three passenger doors on the left side: one forward, one overwing, and one aft—distinct from the 737-900’s four-door layout.
737-800 has engine nacelles with a characteristic oval-to-round cross-section typical of CFM56-powered NG models.
737-800 has a tailcone shape that tapers smoothly to the rudder without the blunt or squared-off appearance of older 737 Classics.
737-800 has wing root fairings that blend smoothly into the fuselage, unlike the more angular junction seen on 737-500/600 models.
737-900: 737-900 has the longest fuselage among all 737 Next Generation variants.
737-900 features low-mounted wings with moderate sweep, consistent with the 737 NG family but visually elongated relative to the 737-800.
737-900 is a twin-engine jet with one turbofan engine mounted under each wing.
737-900 uses high-bypass turbofan engines housed in nacelles suspended from the wings.
737-900 has a conventional tail configuration with a single vertical fin and low-mounted horizontal stabilizers.
737-900 retains the classic 737 nose shape: short, rounded, and slightly upturned compared to the longer, more tapered 757-200 nose.
737-900 has a narrow single-aisle fuselage with a circular cross-section appearance typical of Boeing 737s.
737-900 is a narrow-body airliner, visually distinct from wide-body aircraft like the 767 or 777.
737-900 has main landing gear housed in streamlined pods or fairings under the fuselage, not in large wing-root bays.
737-900 sits lower to the ground than the 757-200 due to shorter landing gear struts.
737-900 has a relatively short-to-medium landing gear height, giving it a low-slung stance compared to the taller 757-200.
737-900 has overwing exits arranged as a single pair per side, fewer than the two-per-side layout on the 737-800.
737-900 exhibits a slender, stretched fuselage profile that appears unusually long for a 737 NG aircraft.
737-900 has winglets that are typically blended or split-style, matching other 737 NG variants but not the plain raked wingtips found on some early models.
737-900 has a compact undercarriage footprint consistent with the 737 family, unlike the wider-track gear of the 757-200.

737-900 has cockpit windows with a distinctive curved upper edge and forward-sloping windshield, shared across the 737 NG series but visually distinct from the 757-200’s flatter, more angular glazing.
737-900 has a fuselage length noticeably greater than the 737-800, creating a more pronounced taper from nose to tail.
737-900 has engine nacelles positioned farther aft along the wing chord than those on the 737-600, reflecting its stretched airframe.
737-900 has a vertical stabilizer height and aspect ratio consistent with the 737 NG family, shorter and squatter than the taller, narrower fin of the 757-200.
737-900 has a fuselage diameter identical to other 737 variants, maintaining the same circular cross-section while extending significantly in length.
747-100: 747-100 has a short upper deck hump that ends just behind the cockpit, unlike the extended upper deck of the 747-300 and 747-400.
747-100 features simple, unmodified wingtips without vertical winglets, distinguishing it from the winglet-equipped 747-400.
747-100 has four underwing engines mounted on pylons spaced far outboard along the swept wings, a hallmark of the 747 family.
747-100 displays a tall conventional vertical tail with horizontal stabilizers mounted low on the fin base, not high-mounted like some newer wide-bodies.
747-100 has a long, pointed nose ahead of the cockpit that creates a distinctive front-fuselage profile absent in narrow-body jets.

747-100 has a very large wide-body fuselage with a circular cross-section, visibly broader than any narrow-body airliner such as the 737 or A320.
747-100 has low-mounted swept wings with pronounced dihedral, contrasting with the high-wing configuration of cargo aircraft like the C-130.
747-100 features main landing gear with four-wheel bogies under the fuselage and two four-wheel bogies under each wing, unlike the simpler gear of smaller jets.
747-100 has a hump-backed upper deck that begins immediately behind the cockpit and rises sharply, setting it apart from the flat-roofed A340.
747-100 has no dorsal fin extension above the vertical stabilizer, unlike the enlarged dorsal fin found on many 747-400s.
747-100 has forward boarding doors located only on the main deck, with no upper-deck passenger doors, unlike the 747-300 and 747-400.
747-100 has a shorter overall fuselage length than the 747-200, though externally nearly identical, with subtle differences in window count near the rear.
747-100 has a narrower wing chord and less complex leading-edge slat configuration compared to the upgraded wings of the 747-400.
747-100 has a single, uninterrupted upper-deck roofline without the extended bubble-shaped section seen on the 747-300.

747-100 has a cockpit windshield with a more angular, less curved profile than the smoother, more blended glazing of the 747-400.
747-100 has a shorter distance between the nose gear and main fuselage gear than the stretched 747-300 and 747-400.
747-100 has ventral fins mounted low on the aft fuselage underside, a feature retained from early 747 design but omitted on some later variants.
747-100 has a distinctively blunt, squared-off trailing edge on the horizontal stabilizer, unlike the rounded tips common on the 747-400.
747-200: 747-200 has a shorter upper deck than the 747-300.
747-200 lacks winglets, unlike the 747-400.
747-200 features four turbofan engines mounted under a low-swept wing.
747-200 has the same fuselage length as the 747-100 but with updated engine nacelles.
747-200 displays the classic Boeing 747 humpback profile with a forehead-shaped cockpit nose.
747-200 has a conventional tail with a single vertical stabilizer and low-mounted horizontal stabilizers.
747-200 has a very large wide-body fuselage with two passenger decks at the front forming a distinct upper-deck hump.
747-200 has main landing gear with multiple bogies under both the fuselage and wings.
747-200 has a longer fuselage than the 747-100 in some early production blocks but retains the original hump length.
747-200 has no wingtip extensions or raked wingtips, distinguishing it from later 747 variants.
747-200 has a long wingspan typical of jumbo-jet proportions, visibly larger than twin-engine wide-bodies like the A330.
747-200 has cockpit windows positioned above the nose, creating a prominent forehead silhouette.
747-200 has a dense multi-wheel landing gear arrangement due to its heavy weight and wide-body design.
747-200 has a low-mounted wing with moderate sweep, consistent across the early 747 family.
747-200 has four large circular engine nacelles, each housing a single turbofan engine.
747-200 has a shorter overall length than the 747-300, visible in side-profile fuselage proportion.
747-200 has no dorsal fin extension beyond the base of the vertical stabilizer, unlike some 747-400 configurations.
747-200 has a standard forward door layout with one main boarding door ahead of the wing and one emergency exit just behind it.
747-200 has a wider fuselage diameter than narrow-body jets such as the 737 or A320, confirming its wide-body classification.
747-200 has the characteristic 747 upper-deck hump extending only partway back along the fuselage, shorter than the full-length upper deck of the 747-300.
747-300: 747-300 has a longer upper deck hump than the 747-200 but shorter than the 747-400.
747-300 features four underwing engines mounted in pairs beneath swept low-mounted wings.
747-300 retains the classic Boeing 747 tail design with a tall single vertical fin and conventional horizontal stabilizers.
747-300 has a very large wide-body fuselage proportionally longer than the 747-100 but shorter than the 747-400.
747-300 lacks the upward-curved winglets found on the 747-400.
747-300 has a partial upper deck that extends farther aft than on the 747-200 but stops well short of the wing trailing edge.
747-300 uses high-bypass turbofan engines typical of 1980s wide-body airliners.
747-300 has main landing gear with four-wheel bogies under the fuselage and two four-wheel bogies under each wing.
747-300 has a distinctive hump-shaped forward fuselage created by the partial upper deck, unlike the flat-fronted Airbus A340.
747-300 has a longer nose section ahead of the cockpit windows compared to the 747-100.
747-300 features three passenger doors on the left side of the forward fuselage, distinct from the four-door layout of later 747-400s.
747-300 has a wing sweep angle identical to the 747-200 but different from the slightly modified wing of the 747-400.
747-300 has a taller vertical tail relative to fuselage height than the DC-10 but shorter than the 747-400’s tail.
747-300 has a wide-body cross-section clearly larger than twin-engine narrow-bodies like the 737 or A320.
747-300 has engine nacelles with circular inlets and no chevrons, distinguishing it from newer-generation aircraft.
747-300 has a cockpit window arrangement with six forward-facing panes, differing from the seven-pane layout of the 747-400.
747-300 has a fuselage cross-section diameter consistent with the entire 747 family, wider than the MD-11’s.

747-300 has a lower fuselage curvature beneath the upper deck hump than the more aggressively blended 747-400 hump.
747-400: 747-400 has prominent vertical winglets at the wingtips, unlike the 747-100, 747-200, and 747-300 which lack winglets entirely.
747-400 features a longer upper deck than the 747-100 and 747-200, extending further aft past the cockpit hump.
747-400 retains the classic four-engine layout with engines mounted in two pairs under the swept wings, distinguishing it from twin-engine wide-bodies like the A340 or 777.
747-400 has a very large wide-body fuselage with a distinctive hump-backed upper deck ahead of the wings, unlike the flat upper deck of the DC-10 or MD-11.
747-400 uses low-mounted swept wings with pronounced raked trailing edges, whereas earlier 747 variants have blunter wing trailing edges.
747-400 has a tall vertical fin with a swept horizontal stabilizer mounted on the fuselage, unlike the T-tail configuration of the L-1011 or DC-10.

A340-300 has a long wide-body fuselage with a single full-length passenger deck, separating it from narrow-body aircraft like the 737 or A320.
